title: What Ganesha rides
hookLine: Ganesha catches a giant mouse and rides it instead of killing it: desire steered, not destroyed
carry: ganesha rides desire; it doesn't ride him
tomorrow: he's always got a sweet in his hand. what is it, and why?
last: LEARNING IS SACRED; GANESHA GAVE A TUSK.

lines: A BIG GOD, A TINY MOUSE.
A MOUSE THE SIZE OF A MOUNTAIN.
cards: Big belly, elephant head, sitting like a king, and under him, carrying all of it, a tiny mouse. Why a mouse?
One well-known telling, from the Ganesha Purana: in the court of the gods, a heavenly musician named Krauncha is careless and steps on a sage's foot. The sage curses him: become a mouse.

But he becomes a mouse the size of a mountain, and he tears through another sage's forest home, eating everything in sight. Ganesha throws his noose, catches the mouse and pulls it close. The mouse gives up.
And Ganesha doesn't kill it. He climbs on.

teach.b: In this tradition, gods have animals that carry them. Shiva rides Nandi, the bull. Vishnu rides Garuda, the great eagle.
Durga rides a lion. Kartikeya, from the race, has his peacock.

teach.h: THE MOUNT SAYS WHO THE GOD IS.
teach.b: The word is vahana, from the Sanskrit root vah, to carry, and a vahana says something about its god. So what does the mouse say?
A reading many teachers give: the mouse is desire. Restless, nibbling, never full, like Krauncha eating his way through the forest. Ganesha doesn't kill it, starve it or chase it out.
He catches it, sits on it and steers it. That's a real thread in Hindu teaching: the senses and their wanting aren't evil, but they make a poor master. You ride them; they don't ride you.

teach.h: A FAST, A VOW, AN OFFERING.
teach.b: Hindus practice this in small ways: a fast on a holy day, a vow to give something up for a season, food offered to God before it's eaten.

teach.h: GANESHA RIDES DESIRE; IT DOESN'T RIDE HIM.
teach.b: The wanting stays. It just stops being in charge. Other Puranas tell the mouse's beginnings differently, and none is the one official story.
What they share is the picture: the wise god on top, the wanting underneath, carrying him where he chooses.

how: In temples and home shrines a god's vahana often sits facing the deity, and Ganesha's mouse sits at his feet. Many Hindus keep fasts (vrat) and small vows as a way of steering desire; some devotees of Ganesha fast on Sankashti Chaturthi each month until the moon rises.

games.q: a friend laughs: a huge god riding a tiny mouse is ridiculous. what's one Hindu reading of it?
o: the mouse is desire, restless wanting. Ganesha doesn't kill it; he rides it and steers it.
the mouse is a pet, there to make the statue cute.
the mouse is Ganesha's enemy, trapped under him forever.
games.why: a vahana shows something about its god. one reading many teachers give: the wanting mind, mastered, not destroyed. the mouse still carries him.

practice: For two minutes, sit still and watch for the mouse. Sooner or later a want will run through: your phone, a snack, the next thing to do. Don't chase it out, and don't obey it.

Just notice it, call it wanting, and let it sit under you while you stay put. If you pray, you can offer that want to Ganesha. Some Hindus do this for a whole day with a fast; two minutes is a fine start.

wordCard.voice: Vahana: the one that carries, the animal each god rides. From vah, to carry. Ganesha's is the smallest of them all, a mouse.

orig.note: Sanskrit: that which carries, a vehicle or mount, from vah, to carry.

carryVoice: For the road: Ganesha rides desire; it doesn't ride him. The mouse carries, and the god steers. Day twenty-seven, carried.

sources.ref: Ganesha Purana (Krauncha, the cursed gandharva, caught by Ganesha's noose and made his mount); Mudgala Purana (other origins of the mouse)
